the volume of micellization changes from positive to negative with increasing hydrostatic pressure for anionic, cational, and nonionic micelles and that the crossover is attributable to a combination of changes in headgroup and tail compressibilities.

we have developed a direct simulation methodology to compute the volume of micellization for a surfactant and have shown that the volume of micelle formation changes from positive to negative with increasing pressure, in agreement with experiment, and have shown that a Kirkwood-Buff analysis permits the breakdown of these micellization volumes into constituent headgroup and tail contributions.

the volumes of micelle formation of an anionic sulfated, a nonionic ethoxylated, and a cationic quaternary ammonium surfactant in water exhibit maxima with increasing pressure and that the volumes of surfactant micelle formation can be broken down into headgroup and tail group contributions using the Kirkwood-Buff formalism.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

pressure-induced changes in the volumes of micelle formation are dominated by changes in the headgroup volume, and that the headgroup volume changes can be understood in terms of changes in the hydration of the polar headgroups.
micelle formation is a pressure reentrant phenomenon.

the volumes of micelle formation are not simply the sum of the volumes of the individual surfactants, but rather the result of complex interactions between the headgroups and tails of the surfactants and the solvent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
surfactants are compressible and their compressibilities are dependent upon the nature of their headgroup and tailgroups.
the volumes of micelle formation are determined by the balance of the hydrophobic effect, which favors the micelle phase, and the hydrophilic effect, which opposes the micelle phase.
pressure reentrant assembly of surfactants in water is due to a combination of headgroup and tail compressibilities, which are in turn due to the nature of the headgroup and tail, respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that

molecular simulations of the pressure-dependent volumes of micellizations of surfactants can be carried out directly, and that the resulting data can be analyzed to provide a detailed understanding of the molecular factors that control the pressure reentrant assembly behavior of surfactants.

the pressure reentrant micellization volume behavior of surfactants is a direct consequence of the pressure dependence of the volumes of transfer of the surfactant monomer components from the aqueous phase to the micellar aggregate, and not the result of any pressure-induced change in the micellization process.
the volume of micellization is a fundamental property that is accessible by molecular simulation and can be used for a deeper molecular-level understanding of surfactant self-assembly.
